observation: A rule can be registered in DefaultRegistry and emit findings while having no entry in FindingMetadataCatalog, and nothing anywhere reports it. php.generic-status-envelopes shipped that way under SLOP-1: the rule fired, the docs described it, the tests passed, and its why/suggestedAction/confidence were simply absent. Enumerating the registry against the catalog shows 23 catalog entries and two registered rules with no entry: php.generic-status-envelopes, and php.magic-numbers, which predates this work entirely. The obvious guard is a test asserting every registered rule has a catalog entry. That test cannot be added to the pull request that introduced the first omission, because it fails immediately on the second one and converts a three-rule feature branch into a historical-debt repair.

evidence.summary: Iterating DefaultRegistry::create()->rules() against the FindingMetadataCatalog constant reported `catalog entries: 23, missing: 2` naming php.generic-status-envelopes and php.magic-numbers.

The SLOP-1 close gates all passed with the omission present: composer run test (136 tests), composer run analyse, composer run scan:self and agent-loop verify were green, and the review blindspots gate reported only an unrelated security-term warning.

PR #34 added the missing php.generic-status-envelopes entry as a side effect of adding entries for its own two rules, and its testAdaptedRulesExposeAgentFacingMetadata asserts only on those rules, so php.magic-numbers stays silently uncovered.

hypothesis: The catalog is a lookup table rather than a required constructor argument, so nothing forces the two to move together. Adding a rule is a four-file change and the catalog is the file with no test pulling on it, which makes it the one that gets forgotten.
validated_conclusion: A registry and a parallel metadata table that are only joined at read time will drift, and the drift is invisible precisely because the read path tolerates a miss. The structural fix is to make the metadata part of the rule contract so a rule cannot exist without it; the cheap fix is a completeness test. Either way the guard has to be introduced in its own change, because a correctness invariant added retroactively fails on every prior omission at once, and attaching that repair to an unrelated feature branch is how a small feature turns into an audit nobody asked for.
